entries.title: DOJ Charges Dozens of Immigrants in California Amid Bitter Elections Battle
entries.summary: A DOJ attorney told reporters that the names of all 28 of those charged were on a thumb drive the DOJ sent to California election officials last week.
entries.content:
The Justice Department announced on Monday that it charged 28 immigrants for voting or registering to vote in a U.S. election, an operation that comes amid a major push by the Trump administration to assert control over the state’s vote-by-mail process.

The DOJ said it began arrests on Monday morning as part of what it called “Operation Protect the Vote.” Eleven people are in custody so far, Bill Essayli, the first assistant U.S. attorney for the Central District of California, said during a Monday press conference.

“Instead of respecting the laws of this nation, they violated the sacred trust by falsely claiming to be U.S. citizens when they're not, registering to vote, and some of them voting, and lying about it under oath when they sought another exercise of grace, naturalization,” Essayli said.

He added that all the immigrants arrested are lawful permanent residents, an immigration status that does not allow people to register to vote or to vote in elections.

California and the DOJ are engaged in a battle over 20,000 people that the agency has identified as possible noncitizen voters. The DOJ sued California last week for not complying with its request to halt or set aside the ballots of those identified.

The administration is now saying that California should not count those 20,000 votes until citizenship is verified, and that election officials who count those votes could be held criminally responsible.

Trent McCotter, the acting deputy attorney general, said during the press conference that the names of all 28 people were on the list sent to California election officials — which was delivered via a password-protected thumb drive, with the password attached on a sticky note.

The correspondence arrived close to two weeks after California began sending mail-in ballots.

But top California officials have remained defiant, with some arguing that the DOJ’s actions during the early voting process is disruptive.

“Their timing is rife with and smacks of and reeks of desperation and bad faith, to do this during an election,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta said on Friday.

California Sen. Alex Padilla sent a letter on Thursday to the DOJ, along with Democratic Sens. Richard Durbin of Illinois and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, asking the agency to “reaffirm its longstanding election non-interference policy and rule out any attempt to seize ballots or any other election materials or equipment before voting, counting, and/or certification are complete.”

The administration continues to ramp up its work to prove that noncitizens are voting in large numbers in California. McCotter added that the DOJ is now seeking an emergency motion for relief in the lawsuit filed last week to “set aside and segregate” 20,000 ballots until citizenship is confirmed.

The 28 people charged by the DOJ remain a miniscule percentage of eligible voters in the state. As of Sept. 4, the state of California had over 23.1 million registered voters.

entries.title: Letters With Suspicious Powder Sent to Politicians Deemed ‘Not Harmful’
entries.summary: Federal investigators are still probing the letters mailed to more around 40 lawmakers, which arrived 25 years after envelopes of anthrax killed five people.
entries.content:
Letters mailed to lawmakers around the country containing suspicious powder were not harmful, according to a notice sent to congressional offices and shared with The Washington Sun on Monday.

The House sergeant at arms “continues to monitor incidents of letters containing a white powder that have been mailed to several Congressional offices,” the notice, sent by Sergeant at Arms William McFarland, said. “None of the letters received by Congressional offices have been determined to contain hazardous substances.”

The FBI, U.S. Capitol Police and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating the letters. Capitol Police and the Postal Service referred questions to the FBI.

“The FBI and U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings sent to various addresses nationwide, including Secretary of State offices and their related election offices,” an FBI spokesperson said in a statement.

As of Monday morning, around 40 members of Congress in both parties had reported receiving the suspicious mail. Lawmakers including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and Sens. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Delaware), Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Pete Ricketts (R-Nebraska) were among those targeted.

Lawmakers across the political spectrum condemned the influx of the letters amid rising political violence in the country. Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota) said in a post on X Friday that his Sioux Falls office was evacuated and closed on Friday after receiving a suspicious letter.

“This situation is deeply concerning and follows a trend of intimidating tactics that impact our team members. This has no place in our nation. America is better than this,” Rounds said.

Rep. Brad Schneider (D-Illinois) called on the FBI to “apprehend and prosecute those responsible” for disseminating the letters.

“Anyone or any group who thinks they can scare or intimidate Members of Congress or our teams from doing our job and work on behalf of the people we represent is sorely mistaken,” he said in a statement.

Rep. Kevin Kiley, an independent who caucuses with Republicans, echoed those calls after his office in Rocklin, California, closed following the delivery of a similar letter.

“No one should have to worry for their safety simply because they go to work for the American people,” Kiley said in a statement. “This incident highlights — once again — why we need to bring down the temperature in our politics and embrace a return to civility and commonsense.”

The FBI said that it is working to respond to each incident and identify the “individual or individuals” responsible, adding “this FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service will continue to safeguard the public and secure elections for American citizens.”

The incident comes exactly 25 years after a series of letters containing anthrax were mailed to Capitol Hill offices in 2001. Those letters were directed to two Democrats — former Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle and former Senate Judiciary Chair Patrick Leahy.

Mailed just weeks after the 9/11 attacks, the letters caused 22 cases of anthrax poisoning and killed five people.

A notice sent to Senate offices on Thursday warned offices about the suspicious packages and advised staffers on how to identify and handle potentially suspicious items. It noted that mail and packages sent to offices in the Capitol complex are screened at off-site locations, a practice begun after the 2001 anthrax attacks.

Many of the lawmakers targeted said that U.S. Capitol Police intercepted the mail before it arrived at their offices, though others received the mail at their state or local offices.

“Thanks to existing safety protocols and the swift action taken by the officers, neither the Senator nor her staff are in any immediate danger,” Blunt Rochester’s office said in a statement.

The suspicious letters also follow a series of mailings to secretaries of state and related election offices in at least 15 states about two weeks until Election Day.

Threats against election workers have increased in recent years — election officials in nearly 20 states received suspicious packages with nonhazardous substances ahead of the 2024 election, and election officials in at least five states received envelopes, some laced with fentanyl, in 2023.

Ohio’s Republican Secretary of State Frank LaRose, whose office received one of the letters on Wednesday, said he would not be intimidated by the threat ahead of the November election, where his office is overseeing a particularly close Senate race.

“We're certainly not distracted or deterred by that kind of thing,” he told The Sun. “It's unfortunate, but law enforcement did what they're supposed to do and we're focused on running good elections for the people of Ohio.”

entries.title: Judge Says There's 'No Universe' Where Tree Removal Isn't Linked to Trump's Golf Course Plans
entries.summary: Judge Ana Reyes questioned the government's plans for East Potomac Park during a contentious hearing.
entries.content:
By Gary Fields

A federal judge hearing testimony Monday on President Donald Trump’s plans to redevelop a Washington golf course expressed deep skepticism over the government’s contention that the recent mass cutting of trees at East Potomac Park and the plans for a new golf course were not connected.

“There is no universe in which all of this coincidentally happened all at the same time,” U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes said during a contentious hearing over the fate of a project that is a key feature of Trump's campaign to leave his personal imprint on the nation's capital.

Reyes last week ordered a halt to the golf course's redevelopment plans until at least Oct. 26 after scolding the government for starting a large-scale tree removal at the course over a holiday weekend while providing little notice to the court or the plaintiffs trying to stop the makeover.

Then, on Sunday, Trump announced plans on social media to close the golf course for 15 months, starting on Nov. 15, and redevelop the 106-year-old park and course despite a court challenge by the D.C. Preservation League and two golfers. In a post on Monday, Trump said the work would start immediately.

Plaintiffs' attorneys challenging the golf course renovation work have asked Reyes to extend her order that temporarily paused the work. They say the work is inflicting irreversible damage.

entries.title: DNC Asks Judge to Stop New MAGA Inc. Midterm Ad From Airing
entries.summary: It’s just the latest development in an ongoing legal saga over a series of White House advertisements that critics have called “propaganda.”
entries.content:
The Democratic National Committee demanded on Monday that a federal judge block another of President Donald Trump’s midterm ads from airing — this one allegedly created by White House staff and paid for by Trump’s super PAC, MAGA Inc.

The process represents a violation of federal law meant to prevent political staff performing campaign-related work, the DNC argued in a new filing.

It’s just the latest development in an ongoing legal saga over a series of White House advertisements that critics have called “propaganda” and comes after a federal judge ordered the Trump administration to stop airing several taxpayer-funded ads through the midterm elections.

“Rather than paying to develop its own advertisement, MAGA Inc. broadcast an ad unlawfully developed by White House Office personnel, whose salaries are paid using Congressional appropriations,” Daniel J. Freeman, the DNC’s litigation director, wrote in the filing submitted Monday.

MAGA Inc. began airing an ad titled “Every Democrat Voted Against No Tax on Tips” over the weekend, but the TV spot is virtually the same as an advertisement posted to the White House’s YouTube channel. Congress enacted the measure in question, which allows workers to deduct up to $25,000 of qualifying tip income on their taxes, through Trump’s “one big beautiful bill” last year.

“This same ad (minus the tag-line indicating MAGA Inc. had paid for airtime) appeared on the Official White House YouTube Channel on October 12,” Freeman wrote, indicating that it was produced by the Trump administration rather than the president’s political organization.

The White House and MAGA Inc. did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The DNC’s lawsuit is one of three legal challenges to the taxpayer funded ads currently pending.

Earlier this month, Judge Jennifer L. Rochon of the Southern District of New York granted a temporary restraining order to block the ads and extended the freeze through Nov. 8 in a separate legal challenge brought by nonpartisan watchdog group Common Cause and a coalition of other plaintiffs.

In response, the Department of Homeland Security assured Rochon it did not have any plans to pursue additional media buys past Oct. 11 — though the ads continued to air for a short time after that date.

Before Rochon temporarily blocked the ads, Trump announced in a Truth Social post on Oct. 5 that he planned to “pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc.” — a move that may violate federal campaign finance laws that prohibit a president from directing spending decisions for a super PAC.

The White House later confirmed that the president would not be reimbursing the federal government for money used for the ads up to that point. In a federal court declaration, a senior DHS official, Holly C. Mehringer, confirmed that LMD Agency had already purchased approximately $19 million in media buys through Oct. 11.

The administration created up to 13 ads, CNN reported, though only several hit the airwaves ahead of Rochon’s restraining order. Each of the previously aired spots contained a disclaimer reading “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”

The ads often feature stylized edits of the president and Cabinet officials, with one spot echoing Republican rhetoric on the dangers of communism and another depicting U.S. missile strikes on Iran.

In previous statements shared with The Washington Sun, the White House characterized the ads as “Presidential Public service announcements” and said that they “are nothing new,” citing ad campaigns run by former presidents George W. Bush, Barack Obama and Joe Biden.

entries.title: AJ Dybantsa Is Still ‘Day-to-Day’ Ahead of the Wizards’ Season Opener
entries.summary: The No. 1 pick sprained his ankle during Friday’s preseason finale against the Pelicans.
entries.content:
AJ Dybantsa’s status remains in doubt as the Wizards prepare for Wednesday’s season opener against the Bucks.

The No. 1 pick in June’s NBA draft sprained his left ankle after landing awkwardly on a mid-range jump shot during the second quarter of Friday’s preseason game against the Pelicans. The Wizards lost, 107–106, to conclude the preseason with a 2–2 record. Dybantsa scored 12 points in 15 minutes before getting injured.

He didn’t return to the game, and Wizards coach Brian Keefe said on Friday that the decision to remove him from the contest was precautionary.

Asked on Sunday if Dybantsa would play against the Bucks, Keefe told reporters, “We’re just going to take it one day at a time.”

Dybantsa was seen shooting free throws at the end of the team’s practice on Monday, and Keefe said the 6-foot-9 forward’s status remains day-to-day.

The Wizards are expected to practice on Tuesday and have a traditional pregame shootaround, giving the coaching staff two more opportunities to evaluate Dybantsa before Wednesday’s opener.

Dybantsa proved durable last year in his lone college season at BYU, playing in 35 games while leading the nation in scoring at 25.5 points per game. His only known ailment with the Cougars was an illness he played through in a January game against TCU.
entries.author: Alex Schiffer

entries.title: Bilal Coulibaly and the Wizards Fail to Reach a Contract Extension
entries.summary: Washington’s second-longest tenured player was eligible for a new four-year deal.
entries.content:
Bilal Coulibaly will be a free agent at season’s end.

The Wizards’ second-longest tenured player failed to reach an agreement with the team ahead of Monday’s 6 p.m. deadline for rookie extensions.

Coulibaly was eligible for a four-year extension at the end of his current rookie deal. Given Coulibaly’s status as a role player, his extension would have likely looked similar to the deals Washington gave to Deni Avdija in 2023 (four years, $55 million) and Corey Kispert in 2024 (four years, $54 million).

Coulibaly was asked about his contract situation at media day last month and said he wasn’t worried about it.

“I'm just focused on basketball,” Coulibaly said. “Just being out here with the guys, it's gonna build chemistry and stuff like that. … I'm not really thinking about everything that comes around, all the talking. Just focused on bettering myself and making the team better, too.”

The 22-year-old is the first player of the Wizards’ young core to be extension eligible. Drafted No. 7 overall by the Pacers in 2023, his rights were traded to the Wizards for Jarace Walker (the No. 8 pick) and two second-round selections. Coulibaly was the first pick made by Monumental Basketball President Michael Winger and Wizards GM Will Dawkins, who were hired a month before the draft.

When Coulibaly was drafted, the 6-foot-7 wing was more known for being the other draft prospect from France’s Metropolitans 92 — his teammate, Victor Wembanyama, went No. 1 overall. In three NBA seasons, Coulibaly has averaged 10.8 points on 43% shooting, but he’s shot just 31% from 3-point range. He’s one of the Wizards best on-ball defenders on a team that has consistently ranked among the league’s worst defensive squads. Coulibaly has also faced injury issues, reaching 60 games played just once in three seasons.

He will make $9.2 million this season in the final year of his four-year, $30 million contract he signed as a rookie. He will be a restricted free agent as long as the Wizards make him a qualifying offer at the start of 2027 free agency. That qualifying offer would be worth $10.3 million.

With Coulibaly’s contract situation settled for now, the Wizards can turn their attention to Anthony Davis, who has been eligible for a four-year, $275 million extension since August. ESPN previously reported that the Wizards and Davis were postponing talks until the quarter mark of the regular season. At media day, Davis said he would decide on his future with the organization “when the season is over.”

entries.title: Trump Defends Waiving Russian Sanctions
entries.summary: The president said it may be time for someone other than Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to negotiate ending the war on Ukraine’s behalf.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump defended his suspension of a set of congressional sanctions against Russia just days before their planned implementation, saying on Monday that imposing the penalties would jeopardize peace negotiations with Ukraine.

Trump said he was “in the midst of negotiating a deal” with Russian President Vladimir Putin on several fronts and framed the waiver as leverage he could reverse at will.

“And of course, we’re negotiating with him on Ukraine. I’m not looking to break up negotiations right in the middle,” he said before departing the White House for Kansas. “And by the way, I have the right to do that at any time, immediately. So if things don’t work out, I can always do it.”

Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18, then rendered most of it unenforceable Friday night, two days before the deadline Congress set for putting it in place.

The law sought to cut off oil and gas revenue financing Russia’s war by imposing tariffs of up to 500% on Russian goods and up to 100% on the largest buyers of Russian crude and on countries helping Russia evade oil sanctions.

Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir Putin earlier this month for Russia to supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter.” Three million tons would follow, depending on the condition of Russian refineries.

Trump used a waiver provision built into the law to suspend those levies, along with other restrictions. Sanctions imposed under earlier executive orders remain in place. The order says the waivers stand until the president or the secretary of state determines otherwise, but it is unclear when the waiver would expire.

He said Monday that he is negotiating with Russia not only on Ukraine but on hostages, diesel and Iran, adding that Moscow has “been very well behaved on Iran.”

“Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way,” he wrote in a Sunday Truth Social post.

Representatives for the White House didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment.

U.S. intelligence officials have assessed otherwise, however. CNN and The Washington Post reported in March that Russia was providing Iran with intelligence on U.S. military targets. When asked at an April Senate hearing if Russia was aiding Iran’s war effort against U.S. forces, Gen. Dan Caine, the Joint Chiefs chair, said there was “definitely some action there.” NBC News reported in August that Russia had transferred drone components and explosives to Iran across the Caspian Sea as recently as July.

Asked about a possible trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump said he was open to one focused on nuclear weapons and suggested it could be held in China during a scheduled November trip for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But talks about Ukraine may not be on the agenda with Xi and Putin.

“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump said Monday. “They haven’t been doing much.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said over the weekend that Russia had launched more than 320 drones at Ukraine’s energy grid over a 12-hour span. Zelenskyy has said that twice in as many weeks, Russian attacks came without advanced intelligence warning from its global partners, including the U.S.

The Trump administration has denied it paused sharing intelligence with Ukraine, something Trump reiterated when asked on Monday. He added that the U.S. has given Ukraine “hundreds of billions of dollars” and gotten “nothing” in return.

Pressed on Zelenskyy’s criticism that the sanctions waiver amounts to backing Putin, Trump said the Ukrainian president “is not helping matters much” and questioned whether Zelenskyy wants the war to end.

Told Zelenskyy had said Trump was on the wrong side of history, Trump said Zelenskyy “doesn’t know what he’s talking about.”

“I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine,” he said.

The comments add to a strained stretch between the two world leaders. Ukraine lost normal access last week to Starshield, the military version of SpaceX’s satellite network that its large drone operations depend on.

Zelenskyy said Sunday on NBC the Starshield slowdown was “a message from the American government” and that “technically, SpaceX did it.”

Trump denied Friday that he or SpaceX CEO Elon Musk were responsible.

Asked Monday who gave the order, Trump said he didn’t know, but he’d “like to find out.”

entries.title: Trump’s $10B Suit Against the BBC Could Offer Jack Smith a Platform
entries.summary: The BBC argues that the former special counsel could discuss evidence related to Jan. 6 that has not been made public.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump’s $10 billion defamation suit against the BBC could give former special counsel Jack Smith a new platform.

The BBC wants Smith — whom Trump has called "a disgrace to humanity” who should be “thrown in prison” over his investigation into the president’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election — to testify in the sprawling lawsuit that already stands to focus harsh light on the president and his inner circle.

The BBC has aggressively used the fact-finding phase of the case to force the president to prove his core claim that he did not incite or foresee the violence on Jan. 6, 2021.

“It is difficult to imagine a more authoritative source on these issues than Mr. Smith, who spent years gathering evidence on those topics with the force of the Justice Department and the power of the grand jury behind him,” the BBC’s lawyers wrote in their motion Monday to subpoena Smith to appear.

Smith has not objected to the subpoena, according to court records, and could be scheduled to appear for a deposition on Dec. 16.

Trump sued in December, seeking $10 billion in damages from the BBC, whose journalists spliced together two different parts of Trump’s Jan. 6 speech, a move that Trump’s lawyers say gave a “misleading impression” of his statements, according to court records.

The BBC has turned the lawsuit against Trump, using it as an opportunity to seek records as part of the discovery process.

Last week, U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett threatened to sanction Trump for backing out of a deposition and repeatedly disregarding court-ordered obligations. The judge has also allowed subpoenas of Donald Trump Jr., Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner. Trump’s private financial records are also being probed.

In the first volume of his final investigative report released on Jan. 14, 2025, Smith concluded that Trump was the "most responsible" and the central figure in the conspiracy to overturn the 2020 election and subsequent Capitol attack.

But much of the evidence uncovered by Smith’s investigation remains under court seal.

"The conclusions of Mr. Smith’s report are public,” the BBC’s lead counsel, Charles Tobin, wrote in the motion. “But the evidence that informed those conclusions is not, including the ‘strong evidence that the violence that occurred on January 6 was foreseeable to Mr. Trump, that he caused it, and that he and his coconspirators leveraged it to carry out their conspiracies.’”

While U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan unsealed a trove of evidence related to the Jan. 6 election-interference case, specific grand jury secrets and unredacted law-enforcement details have yet to be seen by the public.

Smith has testified several times before Congress, facing scrutiny over what Republicans view as abuses by Smith and the Justice Department under President Joe Biden.

In those appearances, he has declined to discuss the sources of his evidence “out of concern for violating criminal procedures,” according to the BBC’s motion.

“In this case, however, Mr. Smith could answer such questions,” Tobin wrote, citing a grand jury rule he asserts “allows for an exception ‘preliminarily to or in connection with a judicial proceeding.’”
entries.author: Gavin J. Quinton
